p.seg: When rain saturates the fields,
or induces millet growth,
immediately report in writing the extent of saturated crops,
induced millet, and the acreage of uncultivated dry fields.
After crops have sprouted and rain falls,
also immediately report the amount of rainfall,
and the acreage benefited.
In cases of drought, violent storms,
flooding,
insect pests,
or other things damaging crops,
also immediately report the acreage affected.
For nearby counties, have swift messengers deliver the reports;
for distant counties, have the postal service deliver them,
all to be completed by the eighth month. [Gap]
Statutes on Agriculture.
In the second month of spring,
do not dare to fell trees in the mountains and forests or block dikes and waters.
Outside the summer months,
do not dare to burn grass for ash at night,
pick unripe lychees,
or take fawns, bird eggs, or fledglings.
Do not use□□□□□□to poison fish or turtles,
set traps or nets,
and release them by the seventh month.
Only those who unfortunately die and require coffins for burial
are exempt from these seasonal restrictions.
In the vicinity of villages, near haystacks, and other prohibited preserves,
do not dare to take dogs for hunting during the fawning season.
If commoners' dogs enter prohibited preserves without chasing or catching animals,
do not dare to kill them;
if they chase or catch animals,
kill them.
Dogs killed in river preserves
must be surrendered intact to the authorities;
for those killed in other prohibited preserves,
consume the meat and surrender the hides.
Statutes on Land Management.
For each qǐng of land, hay and straw are to be submitted,
according to the number of fields received,
whether cultivated or not,
each qǐng shall submit three dàn of hay,
and two dàn of straw.
Hay is accepted from the time it turns yellow and can be bundled.
When submitting hay and straw,
they shall be transported and measured,
and it is permissible.
Statutes on Agriculture.
Grain,
hay and straw are to be cleared from the wood,
matting,
immediately report the quantity in stone to the county court.
If not used,
use the matting again for covering.
Field Statutes.
Those who receive horses or oxen as provisions,
if after two months they have not received them
or delivered them,
shall all cease,
and neither receive
nor deliver them.
For those receiving provisions from the Grand Fields without a permanent register,
they shall be issued on the day the delivery order arrives,
without further delay.
Statute on Fields.
Commoners residing in the fields and cottages shall not dare to distill spirits,
the field overseers and
district assistants shall strictly prohibit and control this,
those who do not comply with the order are guilty.
Field Statutes.
In the fourth month,
seventh month,
tenth month,
and first month, the oxen for field cultivation are to be inspected.
At the end of the year,
a major evaluation is conducted in the first month.
Those who rank highest
are awarded the field overseer with a pot of wine and a bundle of dried meat,
and exempt the drought sufferers from one shift of corvée labor,
granting the ox leader an additional thirty days;
those who rank lowest,
the field overseer is reprimanded,
and the idle stable workers are penalized with two months of labor.
For those using oxen in farming,
if the ox loses weight,
the person in charge is fined ten blows for each tenth of an inch.
There is also an evaluation at the village level,
the top performers
are awarded the field manager an extra ten days, while the lowest
are punished with thirty blows.
Regulations for Stables and Pastures.
If borrowing iron tools,
they become worn out and unusable to the point of being damaged,
prepare a written report,
receive them without penalty.
Stables and pastures.
When herding or pasturing government horses and cattle,
if the horses or cattle die,
promptly report to the county where the death occurred;
the county shall promptly inspect and take them in.
If they are not taken in promptly and allowed to spoil,
order that they be compensated according to their value before spoiling.
If a young slave under servitude dies of illness,
report it to the relevant authorities;
if the death is not due to illness,
report it to the officials with the inspection record for adjudication.
For horses and cattle of the Great Stables,
Central Stables,
and Palace Stables,
their sinews,
hides,
and horns, along with their market price, shall be submitted,
and the responsible person shall report to the relevant office.
If a government horse or cattle used for riding or draft dies in a county,
the county shall inspect and sell the meat collectively,
then submit the sinews,
hides,
and horns,
and also submit the money from the sale.
If the money is less than the legal amount,
order the responsible person to make up the difference and report to the office;
the office shall notify the county of the horse or cattle to write it off.
Now, assess the counties
and capital offices, each with one assessment for government draft cattle;
at the end of the year,
if ten or more cattle and one-third die;
or fewer than ten cattle,
and those responsible for draft cattle have three or more cattle die by year's end,
the officials in charge,
those who feed the cattle, as well as the magistrates
and assistants shall all be held guilty.
The Interior Secretary assesses the counties,
the Grand Granary assesses the capital offices and those responsible for draft cattle.
[Blank].
When grain is stored in granaries,
ten thousand shi are piled together with a thatched door as a household unit.
The county sefu or assistant, together with the granary
and township officials, jointly seal it with their seals,
and leave one door each for the granary sefu and the assistant in charge of grain distribution from outlying towns to ventilate,
sealing it themselves.
All are then issued,
and when the remainder is searched, a new door is opened.
When the sefu is dismissed,
the inspector opens it,
and those who see the joint seals
use the dike to inspect it,
then reseal it jointly.
Do not measure the county,
only those granaries that seal themselves are measured by the county.
When issuing grain,
if it is not from the original deposit, it is issued,
order it to be measured,
and if the measurement matches the dike,
order it to be issued.
If it is insufficient,
the issuer bears the loss;
if there is a surplus,
it is stored.
Do not change when jointly issuing grain.
If the grain stored has not reached ten thousand shi and one wishes to increase the pile,
if the previous depositor is increasing the pile,
it is permissible;
if others are increasing the pile,
the depositor must first measure the original pile,
and if it matches the dike,
then it may be stored.
If later it is found insufficient,
the later depositor alone bears the loss;
and record the name, occupation, and residence of the grain depositor increasing the pile in the granary register.
For piles of ten thousand shi or those not yet full that have been issued from,
do not dare to increase the pile.
In Lìyáng, twenty thousand shi are piled together,
in Xiányáng, one hundred thousand shi are piled together,
their grain receipt and issuance,
and increasing piles follow the statutes.
Senior officials jointly oversee the storage of grain in granaries and its issuance,
seeing the accumulated millet,
rightly pile it,
do not let it spoil.
Granary
When grain crops and
fodder are received,
immediately create a granary register,
and submit it to the Neishi.
‧Fodder is stored in piles of ten thousand shi each,
in Xianyang, twenty thousand shi per pile;
their disbursement,
increase in stock, and inspection follow the same procedures as for grain.
Granary
Grain and
fodder stored in granaries when issued,
any surplus or shortage must be reported to the county court.
If items are issued before being stored yet are already accounted for,
report to the county court,
the court shall order senior officials to jointly seal the granary,
and issue them,
immediately submitting the count to the court;
if the quantity is small,
and one wishes to consolidate it in one county,
it is permissible.
Granaries located in capitals or cities,
should □□□□□□□□□ and be issued jointly.
Granary.
□□□□□ not complete,
order the former officials and new officials to jointly first investigate and issue it.
If the former officials are unwilling,
do not force them.
If there are no former officials,
order the ranked officials,
the clerks in charge,
to jointly issue it with the granary □,
investigate and determine the incompleteness.
Those jointly involved should not be replaced;
if replaced and it becomes incomplete,
order the magistrate,
the assistant to share the compensation for the incompleteness.
Granary
Chéng Hé,
shǔ □□□□ reported the harvest in writing,
separated the quantities,
to distribute to the people.
Granary
Calculate the grain,
separate the yellow,
white,
and green.
Do not distribute it to people.
Granary
After the rice harvest and the grain ripens,
calculate the rice for the following year.
Record the harvested quantity,
separate polished,
glutinous, and non-glutinous rice.
Separate the polished,
glutinous rice's yield,
accumulate it yearly with variations,
do not increase the accumulation,
to supply to guests,
by October document the quantities in writing,
and report to the Neishi.
Granary
The register of those consuming government provisions in the county and other expenses are submitted to the Grand Granary,
together with the annual accounts.
The Capital Offices check the register of those consuming provisions at the time of accounting.
Granary.
Seeds: For rice,
hemp use two and two-thirds dǒu per mǔ,
millet,
wheat one dǒu per mǔ,
glutinous millet,
beans two-thirds dǒu per mǔ,
soybeans half a dǒu per mǔ.
For fertile farmland,
if the amount does not reach these quantities,
it is permissible.
For those with capital,
determine the seeding rate accordingly.
Granary
The county left wheat to be used as seeds,
mixed with grain to store it.
Granary
Twenty dǒu of unhusked millet,
pounded yields ten dǒu of rice;
ten dǒu of polished rice,
ground yields six and two-thirds dǒu of fine rice.
Ten dǒu of wheat,
yields three dǒu of wheat flour.
Beans,
small beans,
and hemp: fifteen dǒu make one shí.
‧For issuing ground rice or polished millet,
ten dǒu are considered one shí.
Granary
Eunuchs,
metropolitan officials,
and metropolitan government personnel who are appointed as generals for imperial missions,
shall have provisions supplied by the county,
with immediate notification to their original supply county,
which shall reduce their provisions accordingly.
Those who have already received provisions
shall be held accountable by their current county of residence.
Granary
Those who have official business in the army and go to subordinate counties,
shall bring their own provisions,
and must not rely on the counties for supplies.
Granary
When a person on monthly rations has already received their provisions but a public envoy has distributed food,
and if they report returning and do not come for the entire month,
stop their provisions for the following first day of the month,
and provide their rations based on the day they return;
officials with salaries are not stopped.
Granary
When driving relay horses,
they are to be fed once with grain;
if they return after completing their task, they are to be fed once with grain,
all shared among eight horses.
As for the number of times they are driven,
it must not exceed one feeding per day.
If the county horses are fatigued from driving,
they are to be given an additional pot of grain.
Granary Statute
Although I have not been employed, I am clothed and fed by the government.
If any commoners wish to borrow [supplies],
lend them,
enabling them to obtain clothing and food.
Officials should then assist them in their affairs.
Statute on Granaries
When Lìchén and Lìqiè perform public labor,
Lìchén receive two dàn of grain monthly,
Lìqiè receive one and a half dàn;
when they do not perform labor,
do not provide rations.
Young Chéngdàn
and Lìchén who work
receive one and a half dàn of grain monthly;
those unable to work
receive one dàn monthly.
Young Qiè
and Chōng who work
receive one dàn, two dǒu, and half a dǒu monthly;
those unable to work
receive one dàn monthly.
Infants without mothers each receive half a dàn;
even those with mothers but whose mothers are performing miscellaneous public labor together with them,
also provide them,
with half a dàn of grain monthly.
Lìchén working in fields
receive two and a half dàn monthly from the second month,
stopping the extra half dàn at the end of the ninth month.
Chōng
receive one and a half dàn monthly.
Lìchén
and Chéngdàn under six chǐ five cùn in height,
Lìqiè
and Chōng under six chǐ two cùn in height,
are all considered small;
those five chǐ two cùn in height
all work.
Cāng
Minor male and female slaves are registered as major male and female slaves in August,
and receive increased rations in October.
Granary
For those sentenced to city dawn labor building walls and other tasks equally laborious as wall-building,
they are to be fed half in the morning and one-third in the evening;
those guarding offices or performing other duties,
are to be fed one-third portions.
For those who are ill,
the food ration is to be determined after deliberation,
and ordered to be managed by an official.
For convicts sentenced to city dawn labor and grain pounding,
grain pounding and supervision by a sīkòu,
or white refined rice punishment engaged in earthwork,
they are to be fed one-third portions;
if not engaged in earthwork,
they are to be fed according to the law.
The granary
Those performing forced labor as "city dawn" convicts during daylight hours,
shall receive full monthly rations until the end of the month, with any surplus used to supplement the rations for the intercalary ninth month.
If "city dawn" convicts engaged in light duties receive increased rations,
the supervising officials shall be judged according to the law governing violation of decrees.
Reduce the monthly rations for "pounding" and "city dawn" convicts when not reaching the full amount.
Granary.
Exempted male and female convict laborers,
male and female convict laborers building walls or performing other tasks equivalent to wall-building,
shall be fed half a sheng in the morning and one-third sheng in the evening for males,
and one-third sheng for females.
Granary
The prisoners are fed,
half a dou per day.
Granary
Raise chickens away from the granary.
For those who use dogs,
keep a sufficient number of dogs.
Regarding pigs and
the offspring of chickens that are not needed,
sell them,
and account for the money separately.
Granary
When government offices receive cash,
one thousand coins are placed in one basket,
sealed with the seals of the Assistant
and the Magistrate.
If the amount does not reach one thousand,
it is also sealed accordingly.
Whether the coins are good or bad,
they are to be mixed together.
When disbursing cash,
the seal is presented to the Assistant
and the Magistrate,
before it can be opened for use.
When common people use cash in the market,
fine and coarse coins are to be mixed,
and they must not dare to differentiate them.
Statute on Gold and Cloth.
Cloth length eight chi,
width two chi five cun.
Cloth inferior,
if its width and length do not conform to the standard,
not to be used.
Jīnbù.
Eleven coins equal one cloth.
When receiving or disbursing coins in lieu of gold
or cloth,
it shall be according to the statute.
Statutes on Gold and Cloth.
Merchants in market stalls and officials of government offices,
must not dare to select currency or
cloth;
those who select currency or
cloth,
if the row leaders do not report it,
or the officials supervise negligently,
all shall be guilty.
Statutes on Currency and Cloth.
When buying or selling,
each item shall be marked with its price;
small articles worth less than one coin each
need not be marked.
Statute on Currency and Cloth.
When officials deliver [goods],
they shall report in writing the year of the outgoing account,
and the recipients shall account for it as the incoming year.
In the eighth
and ninth months, if there are deliveries,
calculate the distance of the delivery location.
If it is impossible to reach the accounting location for the delivery,
□□□□□□□ transfer the account to the following year,
ensuring the accounts do not conflict.
When artisans present deliveries to the government,
they shall all be strictly accounted for in that year.
Jīnbù Laws
Each capital official with ranked clerks and detached office stewards
shall have one provisioner each;
their assistants
and scribes shall share the provisioner;
for every ten persons,
one ox-cart,
and one ox-tender.
For redundant assistants
and scribes of capital offices,
for every ten persons,
one provisioner;
for every fifteen persons,
one ox-cart,
and one ox-tender;
if fewer than ten persons,
they shall share provisioners
and ox-carts with their office heads;
for capital office assistants
and scribes numbering fewer than fifteen persons,
seven or more shall be assigned an ox-cart
and servant,
fewer than seven persons,
three or more shall be assigned one provisioner;
small offices without stewards
shall use this to assign servants
and ox-carts.
For newborn livestock,
feed their mothers one dou of millet daily,
discontinuing after fifteen days,
and separately register them for lending.
Statutes on Currency and Cloth.
If there are debts owed to the government and fines or
redemption payments from those residing in other counties,
immediately transfer the claim to the county where they reside for collection.
If the government owes the common people and has not paid,
also transfer it to their county,
and the county shall pay.
Statutes on Gold and Cloth.
If the common people borrow public property or have debts not yet repaid,
on the day when the debt is to be collected,
and the debt is not collected,
and the person dies;
and if state-owned male and female slaves have lost public property
or livestock,
their food and clothing shall be reduced according to the number of days,
not exceeding one-third,
if the losses are numerous,
calculate it,
and by the end of the year the food and clothing are insufficient to gradually repay,
order them to work it off,
and if they are not ordered to work it off,
and the person dies,
the official superintendent and the responsible clerk shall repay it on their behalf.
Statutes on Currency and Cloth
When a county or
capital official is found guilty of
accounting deficiencies requiring compensation,
after judgment is passed,
the superintendent shall accordingly divide the amount in cash among the responsible officials and junior clerks,
issuing each person a tripartite document,
to be submitted to the minor treasury.
The minor treasury shall then collect the debt.
For those submitting surplus funds,
the office shall also issue a document,
to be submitted.
Such debts must not extend beyond the year.
Those failing to submit payment beyond the year or not complying with the order
shall all be judged according to the law.
Statutes on Gold and Cloth
When an official superintendent is dismissed,
and later reappointed as superintendent,
if he is held accountable for fines or other liabilities from his former position,
and is too impoverished to pay,
gradually reduce his salary
and monthly provisions to repay the debt,
without allowing him to perform labor service;
if he is dismissed,
order him to perform labor service according to the law.
When an official superintendent is dismissed,
and an audit of his office reveals deficiencies,
order him and his subordinate officials to share the responsibility,
in proportion to their involvement.
If an official is held liable for a debt due to his position,
and dies before repayment,
or is imprisoned for a crime,
cancel his share.
If he has already paid his share and then dies,
or is permanently assigned to government work to repay a debt,
or if a herdsman in charge of public livestock kills
or loses them,
and dies before repayment or before completing labor service,
all such debts are canceled,
and the wife
or co-residents shall not be held liable.
Statutes on Currency and Cloth
The counties and
metropolitan offices shall, in the seventh month, dispose of public utensils that cannot be repaired.
Those with old markings shall be erased.
Gold and iron objects shall be melted down for bronze.
Metropolitan offices shall deliver them to the grand storehouse,
which shall accept and purchase them,
all to be completed by the end of the seventh month.
Metropolitan offices far from the grand storehouse shall deliver them to the county,
which shall accept and purchase them.
If there are items that cannot wait until the designated time for disposal,
request to purchase them first,
and report the details in writing to the interior history at that time.
For all items that cannot be sold but can be used as firewood or coverings,
use them;
if not usable,
then burn them.
Statutes on Metal and Cloth.
Carriage,
large cart wheels,
if the protective covering is askew,
it is permissible.
Leather,
red lacquerware should be mutually repaired.
Take those that cannot be repaired,
then discard them.
Treasury regulations.
Those receiving clothing
shall draw summer garments from the end of April through June,
and winter garments from the end of September through November.
Do not issue beyond these times.
Winter clothing for the coming year shall be accounted for later.
Prisoners suffering from cold shall be provided with coarse garments.
For one set of coarse cloth,
use three jīn of hemp.
Coarse garments shall be issued as clothing:
one large coarse garment,
uses eighteen jīn of hemp,
worth sixty coins;
one medium coarse garment,
uses fourteen jīn of hemp,
worth forty-six coins;
one small coarse garment,
uses eleven jīn of hemp,
worth thirty-six coins.
After clothing has been issued,
if there are more than ten surplus coarse garments,
deliver them to the Dànèi,
along with the accounting.
Capital offices may use□□□□their offices,
Lìchénqiè,
Chōngchéngdàn shall not use.
Those in Xiányáng shall have their clothing sent by the Dànèi,
those in other counties shall have clothing sent to the county where they work.
The county,
and Dànèi shall both heed their offices' directives,
and issue clothing according to the law.
Jīnbù
Those receiving clothing provisions—
male convicts,
government servants without wives, and convict laborers—
in winter receive one hundred and ten coins per person,
in summer fifty-five coins;
the younger ones in winter receive seventy-seven coins,
in summer forty-four coins.
Female convict laborers in winter receive fifty-five coins per person,
in summer forty-four coins;
the younger ones in winter receive forty-four coins,
in summer thirty-three coins.
Aged or young male and female convicts who cannot clothe themselves,
receive clothing like the female convict laborers.
‧Those who flee,
or are disloyal to their masters or the government,
receive clothing like the male and female convicts.
Jīnbù
For tasks and government markets,
receiving money must immediately deposit it into the money box,
ensuring market participants witness the deposit,
those who disobey the order shall be fined one suit of armor.
Customs and markets
For vessels of the same kind,
their sizes,
lengths,
widths and thicknesses must be uniform.
Artisan's law.
The county and official workshops shall listen to the authorities for calibrating the standard weights,
bushels,
and pecks,
no more than once a year for the jars.
Those with craftsmen need not be calibrated.
If on loan for testing, then calibrate.
Regulations for Artisans.
Corvée laborers within the state and public affairs officials' residences,
if they borrow public [property],
and if there are deaths among those who borrowed,
shall also order their subordinates
and retainers to assume responsibility for the borrowed [property],
as if following military expedition duties.
Statute on Artisans
Official armor and weapons shall each be inscribed with their office name as a permanent mark,
those that cannot be permanently inscribed,
shall be written with cinnabar or lacquer.
When borrowing commoners' armor and weapons,
the permanent mark must be recorded,
and they shall be received by this mark.
If returned borrowed items lack a permanent mark or do not bear the mark of the respective office,
they shall all be confiscated by the government,
and handled according to the provisions of the loan law.
Artisan
Public implements are marked for long-term use,
for a long time.
Those that cannot last long,
are marked with lacquer for durability.
If someone borrows a public implement,
and returns it,
it must be accepted only after verifying the mark.
If it is worn out and worthless,
the mark is removed.
The official shall inform the borrower: If the implement is worn and the mark is feared to be removed,
before it is removed,
request to replace the mark.
If the mark is removed and cannot be identified,
order compensation.
For the borrower,
if their service has ended or they are dismissed,
the official shall reclaim the borrowed item,
and failure to promptly reclaim it is an offense.
‧If the borrower dies,
or is guilty but not held liable,
the clerk shall compensate.
Do not arbitrarily borrow public implements;
those who arbitrarily borrow public implements commit an offense.
Those who damage public implements or [illegible] shall be ordered to compensate.
Lìchén,
xiàlì,
Chéngdàn working with artisans in winter production,
set reduced work quotas,
assigning them three days' work equivalent to two summer days.
Artisans' Work Quotas
Two ordinary female convict laborers are equivalent to one artisan,
four rotating female convict laborers are equivalent to one artisan,
five young male and female convict laborers capable of working are equivalent to one artisan.
Artisan quotas.
Female convicts and women using needles for embroidery and other tasks,
one woman is equivalent to one man.
Artisan Quotas
When new artisans first begin their work,
they produce half the output in the first year,
and thereafter their annual production equals that of experienced artisans.
If the master artisans provide good instruction,
experienced artisans can complete their training in one year,
while new artisans require two years.
Those who complete their training ahead of schedule may report to the superior,
and the superior will reward them accordingly.
Those who fail to complete their training within the allotted time
shall have their names recorded and reported to the Neishi.
Equal Work
If a male slave has skills that can make him a craftsman,
he should not be made to serve as a personal attendant
or cook.
Equally.
When the court issues a conscription order,
failure to comply
incurs a fine of two suits of armor.
Being late by three to five days
results in a reprimand;
six days to ten days,
a fine of one shield;
exceeding ten days,
a fine of one suit of armor.
Those who are captured,
shall be sent for trial.
In case of rain,
conscription is exempted.
When conscripting laborers to build walls within the city,
they are ordered to complete the walls within the year.
If the walls collapse before completion,
the Director of Works and the gentleman in charge of the walls are held guilty,
and their laborers are ordered to rebuild them,
not counting as corvée labor.
For county-maintained forbidden enclosures,
and public horse and cattle pastures,
conscript laborers to cut through walls for gaps and repair them,
immediately reporting to the enclosure officials,
who inspect them.
If they collapse or breach before the year ends,
the county is ordered to conscript laborers again,
not counting as corvée labor.
If they breach or collapse after the year ends,
exceeding three wall sections,
the county maintainers repair them;
for fewer than three sections,
or if before the year ends there is theft or breach allowing entry or exit,
the enclosure officials are ordered to repair it themselves.
For county-maintained forbidden enclosures near mountains,
or distant mountains,
where the soil is poor and cannot withstand rain,
if there is damage in summer,
do not repair it gradually,
but wait until autumn when there is no rain and use corvée labor for it.
For areas near fields where animals or horses and cattle might emerge to eat crops,
the county magistrate shall conscript those with fields nearby,
regardless of status,
providing labor according to field size,
to build walls for repair,
not counting as corvée labor.
Counties must not arbitrarily damage or alter public buildings, government offices, or courts;
if there is a desire to damage or alter them,
it must be reported.
If intending to use convict laborers to expand public buildings, government offices, or repair them,
proceed,
no report needed.
When the county engages in regular tasks or reported actions,
officials set work quotas,
exceeding or falling short by two days or more,
is considered negligence.
For projects initiated by superiors,
if the work quotas are inappropriate,
the county is treated similarly.
Measuring work must involve the Director of Works and artisans together,
not artisans alone.
If inaccurate,
the measurers are judged according to law,
and the actual labor is counted as corvée labor.
Corvée Law
If the county
or capital offices use zhen wood
or zai wood for support beams,
and if the stands for the county bells, when transported,
all prove inadequate and break;
or if the shafts of large carts are inadequate,
and break at the axle,
in all such cases, they are to be discarded as unusable.
The Director of Works
If government offices borrow government-owned carts and oxen... borrowed from others.
If someone privately uses government carts and oxen,
or borrows others to feed the oxen improperly,
the oxen become emaciated;
if the carts are not maintained and repaired,
the carts become damaged and lost,
the large cart axles break;
and if the carts are not cleaned,
the cart covers and canopies forcibly break and split,
those in charge of the carts and oxen as well as the clerks,
and officials in charge shall all be held guilty.
The Minister of Works.
Officials in charge and clerks using government carts and oxen to draw their monthly provisions and the provisions for government oxen and riding horses,
is permissible.
Those in government offices with money shall themselves purchase grease
and glue,
those without money shall monthly report for grease
and glue,
on schedule.
For ironwork repairs,
to repair government large carts.
The Minister of Works.
One portion of grease,
for repairing a large chariot's gaps, one vehicle,
uses one liǎng of glue,
and two portions of grease.
When repairing its loose parts,
apply the glue in several portions accordingly.
For the chariot, do not skimp on the appropriate amount of grease.
Sīkōng.
Order the counties and capital offices to obtain willow and hard wood suitable for writing,
cut them into tablets for writing;
if unavailable, then use wooden boards.
In counties with abundant mountain rushes,
use rushes to bind the writings;
where rushes are unavailable, use cattails,
or common reeds with hemp stalks to tie them.
Each shall accumulate these materials in their respective seasons.
Sīkōng
Those who are guilty and pay fines for redemption or have debts to the public,
shall be interrogated on the appointed day;
if they cannot pay and compensate,
they shall labor on the appointed day,
earning eight coins per day;
if publicly fed,
they earn six coins per day.
Those laboring in government offices and publicly fed,
men receive three portions,
women receive four portions.
Commoners and below who labor to redeem punishments for crimes
or death penalties,
shall labor as convicts in construction or milling,
without wearing red clothes,
and without fetters or cangues.
Convicts performing forced labor,
lower officials without shaving punishments,
and male or female slaves laboring to redeem fines or debts as convicts,
all wear red clothes,
with fetters and cangues,
and are supervised;
if any escape,
it is a crime.
Protected sons and above laboring to redeem punishments up to death penalties,
shall labor in government offices,
and none shall be supervised.
If not interrogated and long imprisoned,
the senior steward,
assistant, and office stewards are guilty.
Those laboring for fines or redemption debts wishing substitutes,
if age and strength match,
it is permitted.
Artisans and merchants in debt,
cannot have substitutes.
If one household has two or more laboring for fines or debts with no one to oversee the home,
release one person,
ordering them to take turns laboring.
Those laboring for fines or redemption debts,
if wishing to register others to labor together,
it is permitted,
without exempting corvée or garrison duty.
‧All who cannot clothe themselves,
the public shall clothe them,
ordering them to labor for the clothing according to law.
If the days are incomplete but money is paid,
it is permitted.
Those using days to offset punishments but unable to feed or clothe themselves,
shall also be fed and clothed and ordered to labor.
If government work for laboring fines or debts is far from the accounting office,
by the end of August, report the labor days and clothing amount to the accounting office,
arriving at the office no later than September;
if offices are adjacent,
by the end of September report to the accounting office,
calculating the labor year.
Commoners with fines or redemption debts having one male or female servant,
or one horse or ox,
and wishing to labor,
it is permitted.
Administer accordingly.
State-owned male and female slaves,
Sīkòu convicts performing hard labor or pounding grain,
and those serving hard labor or pounding grain to repay debts or ransom fines,
shall not be provided with clothing and food;
those working together with convicts performing hard labor or pounding grain,
shall be provided with clothing and food like those convicts.
If a state-owned male slave has a wife,
and the wife is a free commoner or an outsider,
he shall be provided with clothing.
If a private male or female slave is assigned to hard labor or grain pounding,
and borrows clothing and food from the government,
but dies before completing the required days,
the clothing and food shall be deducted.
Director of Constructions.
Those sentenced to wall-building for men and grain-pounding for women,
if their food provisions are to be charged,
shall pay thirty coins per shi.
The Director of Works
Those who reside to pay fines or redeem debts shall return to farming,
allocating twenty days each for sowing
and tending seedlings.
The Minister of Works
Those sentenced to chéngdàn or chōng shall wear red garments,
cover their heads with red scarves,
and be restrained with shackles and manacles.
Common chéngdàn convicts need not be supervised;
those designated for supervision
shall be supervised accordingly.
When chōng or chéngdàn convicts are sent out for labor,
they are forbidden from going to markets or staying outside market gates;
if their route should pass through a market,
they must detour
and avoid it.
If chéngdàn or chōng convicts break earthenware,
ironware,
or woodenware,
or damage axles while building carts,
they shall be punished immediately.
For damages worth one coin,
they shall receive ten strokes;
for damages worth twenty coins or more,
they shall be severely punished,
and the broken item shall be confiscated.
If punishment is not administered promptly,
the official in charge shall bear half the liability.
Sīkōng
The Minister of Justice shall not appoint them as servants,
attendants,
guardians of government offices, or for any other duties.
If there is an order from above to appoint them,
it must be reported again for approval.
The Minister of Public Works
If among the common people there is a mother or sibling who is a female convict slave,
and though not guilty of a capital crime, one wishes to serve as a non-regular conscript on the frontier for five years,
without being credited for the days of service,
in order to free one person to become a commoner,
this is permitted.
‧ Alternatively, if redeeming by commuting the sentence,
and wishing to pay money instead,
the rate is eight coins per day.
Director of Works
Military service shall be rewarded with merits and awards.
Those who die before being officially appointed,
or are guilty and sentenced to shaving their beards as punishment,
as well as those subject to such punishment,
shall not receive their rank or awards.
For those already appointed,
who die before receiving their awards or are sentenced to shaving their beards,
the awards shall be canceled.
Military Rank Law
Those wishing to return two ranks of nobility to exempt one person from being a male or female slave for their parents,
and male slaves who behead enemies to become gōngshì,
who petition to return their gōngshì rank to exempt their former wife from being a female slave,
are permitted to do so,
exempting them to become commoners.
Artisan slaves who behead enemies or have others behead enemies on their behalf to gain exemption,
are all ordered to become artisans.
Those who are physically incomplete,
are made concealed government artisans.
Military ranks
The counties,
metropolitan areas,
and twelve commanderies shall dismiss clerks and assistants,
as well as various subordinate officials,
starting from the first day of the twelfth month,
and concluding by the end of the third month.
In cases of death or vacancies due to other reasons,
replacements shall be appointed,
without waiting for the designated period.
Statute on the Appointment of Officials
Appointment of officials and
commandants,
once appointed,
shall then be ordered to assume duties and dispatched;
those who should not be appointed but dare to assume duties beforehand,
and those who collude in assigning them,
shall be judged according to the law.
When a steward is sent to serve in another office,
he must not appoint his former subordinate officials
and clerks to the new office.
Statute on the Establishment of Officials
If the official in charge is not present,
have an unblemished gentleman or a scribe act as the temporary official,
and do not allow an assistant official
or a clerk to act as the temporary official.
Statute on the Appointment of Officials
When an official assistant or
clerk is dismissed,
transferred,
the official in charge must together with the departing person hand over and inspect with the successor.
If the official in charge is dismissed and the inspection
reveals deficiencies,
the successor and the remaining officials shall be held responsible.
If the former official fails to hand over,
and the new official has not served a full year,
the departing person and the remaining officials shall be held responsible,
the new official shall not be held responsible;
if it is a full year,
even without handover,
the new official and the remaining officials shall be held responsible,
the departing person shall not be held responsible,
other matters follow the statutes.
Inspection
If grain and millet stored in granaries become spoiled,
and accumulated grain and millet rot,
when the amount unfit for consumption is less than one hundred shi,
the official in charge shall be reprimanded;
if it is from one hundred shi up to one thousand shi,
the official in charge shall be fined one suit of armor;
if it exceeds one thousand shi,
the official in charge shall be fined two suits of armor;
the official in charge
and subordinate clerks shall jointly compensate for the spoiled grain and millet.
Even if the grain and millet are spoiled but still edible,
assess them,
and calculate the compensation based on the amount of loss per shi.
Verified.
If the measurement of grain,
hay, and straw falls short by less than one-tenth,
order the restoration of the original amount;
if it exceeds one-tenth or more,
first demand restitution from the person in charge,
and then apply the law to address the shortfall.
Verified.
When grain is received,
ten thousand shi are stored in one pile with the stacks arranged in rows to form a household unit,
and it is recorded as follows:
"The granary contains so-and-so many shi of grain,
Granary Superintendent So-and-so,
Assistant So-and-so,
Clerk So-and-so,
Grain Distributor So-and-so."
If it is received by the county,
the County Superintendent or Deputy,
together with the granary and township officials,
jointly affix their seals to seal it,
and leave one copy each with the Granary Superintendent and the Assistant in charge of grain distribution at the outlying granaries,
for supplying people.
When grain is issued,
there is a record of the issuance,
similar to the procedure for receiving grain.
Verified.
When the granary officer is dismissed and an audit is conducted,
the auditor shall inspect the seals and dikes,
and perform the audit accordingly.
Do not measure the grain in the county,
only the granary's own sealed grain is to be measured in the county.
At the end of the year, prepare a summary statement as follows:
"Such-and-such granary has dispensed so many shi of grain,
with so many shi of grain remaining.
For the granary officer, assistants,
and clerks,
if any are dismissed or leave,
the new granary officer,
new assistants,
and clerks in charge of the granary,
must measure the grain according to the granary register.
If there are any doubts,
report to the county officer,
who shall order someone to remeasure and jointly dispense it.
If there is surplus grain,
it shall be entered,
and those responsible for shortages shall be dealt with according to the law.
Audit.
Grain and
fodder stored in granaries,
if there is a surplus or
a shortage that is concealed and not reported,
and those who transfer the surplus to cover up the shortage,
or falsely issue other goods that should be compensated to offset the shortage,
shall all be treated the same as thieves under the law.
The Chief Scribe and
Assistant Officials who are aware of the offense but do not punish it,
shall be judged according to the law for leveling penalties against offenders,
and shall jointly compensate for the shortage with the person in charge of the granary.
At the time of accounting, the granary records shall be submitted to the Minister of the Interior.
When grain is received or
a leaky granary is opened,
senior officials must jointly supervise and witness it.
The same applies to fodder as to grain.
Verified.
If public vessels are deficient or
incomplete,
they shall be judged and rewarded according to the regulations on compensation,
and those without compensation shall be rectified.
Inspection.
If public vessels are not engraved in a timely manner,
the official in charge shall be fined one shield.
Regulations.
For the messengers of the imperial censor's subordinates,
provide half a dou of refined rice,
one-quarter sheng of sauce for four horses,
vegetable soup,
and supply them with leeks and scallions.
For those who hold a noble rank,
from Guānshìdàfū and above,
provide food according to their rank.
For the attendants of the messengers,
provide half a dou of coarse rice;
for servants,
one-third dou.
Regulations on Provisions for Courier Stations
From Bugeng down to Mourén,
one dǒu of refined rice,
half a shēng of sauce,
vegetable soup,
and half a shí each of hay and straw.
Eunuch officials are treated the same as Bugeng.
Regulations for Meals Provided by Post Stations
Those from Shàngzào rank down to officials and assistants,
clerks without rank,
as well as diviners,
scribes,
charioteers,
attendants,
and storehouse keepers,
receive one dǒu of coarse rice,
vegetable soup,
and two-twenty-seconds shēng of salt.
Regulations for Meals Provided During Travel
For urgent official documents and those marked urgent,
they must be delivered immediately;
for non-urgent ones,
they should be processed daily,
and must not be retained.
Those who retain them will be punished according to the law.
When delivering or transmitting documents,
or receiving documents,
the date and time of dispatch and arrival must be recorded,
to be reported accordingly.
If a document is lost,
report it to the authorities immediately.
Do not assign Lìchénqiè who are elderly, weak, or unreliable.
For documents from the court requiring a response,
if the expected recipient fails to arrive,
pursue them.
Document delivery.
Each county shall notify all offices located within its jurisdiction,
to transcribe the laws applicable to their respective functions.
Internal Administrative Affairs
When there are matters to request,
they must be submitted in writing,
not orally requested,
nor requested [in any other way].
Internal Affairs Miscellaneous Regulations
If an official overseer is dismissed,
□□□□□□□ his office must promptly appoint an overseer.
If more than two months pass without appointing an overseer,
the magistrate and
assistant magistrate are considered to have disobeyed the order.
Internal Administrative Regulations
Except for those who are strong and above,
do not exempt newly registered common soldiers.
If the park steward is not present,
the county shall appoint an acting official,
as per the Stable Regulations.
Internal Administrative Affairs.
Officials not holding the position of scribe shall not serve in government offices.
Those who are not sons of scribes,
shall not dare to study in the study chambers,
and those who violate the order shall be deemed guilty.
Miscellaneous Regulations of the Internal Affairs
Clerks capable of writing
shall not dare to engage in the affairs of scribes.
Internal Administrative Regulations
Where there are government offices that measure materials,
each shall have standard scales and weights,
measuring vessels,
and deadlines.
The offices shall account for them,
and not borrow from the common people.
Those not in use
shall be regulated the same as those in use.
Miscellaneous Records of the Nèishǐ
If there is a substantial office, its walls should be heightened.
Other walls connected to it,
only heighten those storing fodder barns and granaries with thatched covers.
Order people not to rest nearby.
Unless they are the officials in charge,
no one dares to stay there.
Maintain diligent guard duties,
close the gates and extinguish nearby fires promptly,
be cautious in guarding with utmost respect.
If there is disobedience to orders and desertion,
damage occurs,
or a fire breaks out,
the officials will be severely punished,
the Grand Sèfū,
and the Chéng bear responsibility.
Internal History Miscellaneous.
Do not dare to bring fire into the treasury
or the document repository.
After the clerks have collected the stored items,
the official overseer and clerks shall take turns patrolling the offices at night.
When there is no fire,
then close the doors.
Order the scribes to inspect their administrative offices.
When newly constructing clerks' quarters,
do not place them adjacent to the treasury
or the document repository.
Internal Administrative Regulations
Suì Chóu enacted laws at the Censorate.
The Commandant's Miscellaneous Duties
When officials transfer enslaved men and women,
and confiscated persons,
they must record the year, month, and day of their last provisions,
whether they have received clothing or not,
and whether they have wives or not.
Those who receive them shall continue providing food and clothing according to the law.
Attached to the Dependent State.
